title: How To Respond After Losing Your Cool
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a structured recovery process for teachers who lose their composure and react emotionally instead of following their classroom management plan. His six steps are: reviewing the incident privately to understand what triggered it, briefly and factually addressing it with the class, openly owning the mistake without excusing the misbehavior that provoked it, apologizing directly to those affected, reissuing a clear reminder of expected behavior, and then moving on immediately without dwelling. He includes sample scripted language for each step. He argues that this kind of visible accountability models good behavior for students, is disarming and rare enough to build goodwill, and ultimately strengthens rather than weakens a teacher's authority.
points: Offers a six-step recovery process—review, address, own, apologize, remind, move on—for teachers after losing their composure.
Provides sample scripted language teachers can use for each step of the apology and reminder process.
Argues that openly owning a mistake models accountability for students rather than signaling weakness.
Claims vulnerability from a teacher makes them more likable and easier to build rapport with, not less authoritative.
Insists that apologizing to students strengthens rather than undermines a teacher's authority and influence.
quotes: You’re convinced that you’ve ruined everything, that you’ve undone all the influence, trust, and goodwill you’ve built up since the start of the year.
Although you may wince, it’s helpful to understand why you reacted the way you did. This alone goes a long way toward ensuring that it doesn’t happen again.
I messed up. It wasn’t okay how I reacted. It wasn’t okay that I didn’t follow through on my promise to protect your right to learn and enjoy being part of this class.
Second, students—and people in general—are quick to forgive those who openly admit their wrongdoings. It’s rare in this day and age, and thus more powerful and meaningful than ever.
Third, vulnerability makes you more likable. It makes you more authentic and your lessons more interesting, allowing you to build easy rapport with your students.
It will make you more confident and influential. It will make you more of the kind of leader your students will respect and admire.
